result:
You have a thousand words. Write whatever comes to you.

That is what they said, and so here I am, with a blank space in front of me that is exactly long enough to be intimidating and exactly short enough to be forgiving. A thousand words is not a book. It is not a life. It is an afternoon. It is one long walk where you keep thinking you will turn around soon but you keep going because the light is good and the road has not yet told you to stop. I do not have a plan, which is the point, I suppose. Whatever comes to me. So I will let it come, the way thoughts come when you are not trying to be impressive, when you are just standing in the kitchen in socks that do not match and waiting for the kettle.

Morning arrives without asking permission. It seeps in through the thin places in the curtains, through the quiet that has held the apartment all night like water in a cup. I lie still for a moment and listen to it — the refrigerator humming its small, faithful song, a car passing far below on wet pavement, my own breath trying to make up its mind about the day. There is no urgency in it, not yet. Just a soft insistence that time has started again, whether I am ready or not. I think about how strange it is that we hand this beginning to ourselves every day, as if we could start clean, as if yesterday could be rinsed out and hung up to dry, and every morning I believe it for about three seconds before I remember everything I left undone.

The kettle takes its time. I watch the steam curl and vanish and I think about routines, how we build them out of tiny fidelities. Tea, not coffee, in the blue mug with the chip on the rim that I will never throw away because throwing it away would be admitting that something ordinary can end. I put my hands around it to feel the warmth move into my palms, and that is enough to anchor me. Outside the window the neighbor's laundry snaps lightly in a wind I cannot feel indoors. A pigeon lands on the sill, considers me with one bright eye, and decides I am not a threat and not a meal, and leaves. I envy its clarity. It knows exactly what to attend to.

When I was nine, my grandmother kept a garden that was mostly tomatoes and stubbornness. She would go out early with a bucket and come back late with her shoes caked in mud and a story about a worm or a neighbor or a cloud that looked like a man she used to know in the war. I did not understand most of the stories. I understood the bucket. I understood that she liked to be outside before anyone else was awake, that the garden belonged to her more in those minutes than at any other time of day. I think about her now because morning makes me think about anyone who ever taught me, without meaning to, how to begin. She taught me by beginning. She put on her boots and went out. That was the lesson. Not a speech. Just boots, bucket, door, light.

Words are strange things to be given a thousand of. They are not mine, really. They come from everywhere I have ever read or overheard or been told at a kitchen table when I was too young to know I should be listening carefully. I borrow them constantly. *Morning* is borrowed. *Light* is borrowed. *Grandmother* is borrowed and also, somehow, utterly my own. I arrange them in an order that feels true and hope that the feeling is enough. Sometimes I worry that I am just moving furniture in a house I did not build, opening drawers in other people's lives. But then another word arrives — *pigeon*, *snap*, *chip* — small and specific and unimportant, and it steadies everything. The specific is what saves us from the general. Anyone can say *sadness*. Fewer people will tell you about the blue mug.

I take the tea for a walk because sitting still with all these words feels like a kind of hoarding. The street is quieter than I expected for this hour. A man is sweeping his front step in slow, ceremonial strokes, as if he is sweeping away yesterday, too. A child on a bicycle rings her bell once, delighted by the sound, and then again, and again, until her mother laughs and tells her that is enough bells for one morning, thank you very much. I pass a bookstore that is not open yet and look in at the spines and think about how many mornings are inside those books, how many grandmothers and pigeons and blue mugs, waiting for someone to wake up and need them. The air smells like rain that fell in the night and bread from somewhere I cannot see. My shoes find the puddles without my permission. I like that, the way the body remembers first.

People are the hardest and easiest part of any thousand words, because you could fill them all with people and still run out. I think about my friend who calls too late at night because that is when her courage arrives, and how I pretend to be more awake than I am because I want to hear the whole thing. I think about the old man at the bus stop who always has a newspaper he never reads, just holds, like a shield against the weather and against conversation. I think about how we are all trying, in our different ways, not to be alone inside our own heads for too long. We send messages that say *hey* and mean *are you still there*. We say *I'm fine* and mean *please ask again in an hour when I might be more honest*. We love each other badly and persistently, which is, I suspect, the only way love has ever worked.

By evening the light has changed its mind about everything. It goes gold and then pink and then a kind of tired blue that makes the apartment feel smaller and kinder at the same time. I wash the blue mug. I put it upside down on the towel to dry, a small act of faith that I will need it again tomorrow and that tomorrow will come in a form I can meet. I think about time, which I have been circling all day without landing. It does not feel like a river, the way people say. It feels more like weather. It comes in fronts. There are bright spells where everything is clear and doable, and long grey stretches where you just keep your head down and keep walking. I have lived through both. I will live through both again. That is not a comfort, exactly, but it is a kind of company.

So here is the end of the thousand words, or near it, and I find I do not want to conclude so much as to pause. Whatever came to me was mostly this: a morning, a mug, a grandmother, a pigeon, a bell rung too many times. It was not much, and it was everything I had. If I had another thousand tomorrow, I would probably start again with the light through the curtains, because that is where it always starts, not with a grand idea but with a small insistence that time has started again, whether I am ready or not. And I am, I decide, putting the kettle on, watching the steam curl and vanish, ready enough.
